summary: For learners aged 9–11, build the meta-understanding that scientific knowledge is the best current explanation given available evidence — provisional, not final — and that revising ideas when better evidence arrives is science working as intended, a strength rather than a failure. The central worked case is the shift from a geocentric to a heliocentric model, driven by specific observations (retrograde/looping motion of Mars, phases of Venus, Jupiter's moons). Learners should drive a revision themselves by feeding evidence into an accepted model and seeing it strain and be replaced, hear the human/affective side through in-role dialogue, survey a gallery of recurring revisions across sciences, and crucially distinguish 'best-supported but open to revision' from 'just an opinion / anything goes'. Past scientists should be shown as reasonable given their evidence, not foolish, and ideas as holding because of evidence, not authority. The replacement model is itself presented as a new best-current explanation, still open to future revision — not a final, perfect answer.
misconceptions: Thinking that if science changed its mind, it must have been 'wrong' and can't be trusted.
Believing scientific knowledge is a fixed, finished set of facts.
Confusing 'provisional / open to revision' with 'just a guess' or 'anything goes'.
Assuming ideas change because of a powerful person's opinion rather than new evidence.
Viewing past scientists as foolish rather than reasonable given their evidence.
Thinking a well-established theory is beyond all possibility of revision.

activities.title: The 'Best Idea So Far' machine: overturn a model with evidence
steps: Start with the accepted model: Earth sits still at the centre and everything circles it — note that at first it seems to work, so you accept it.

Feed observations into the model one at a time from an evidence tray and judge for each whether the current model fits it or not: 'Mars sometimes loops backwards across the sky' (the geocentric model needs an awkward extra circle to cope), 'Through a telescope, Venus shows phases like the Moon' (a model with Venus circling Earth cannot fit the full set of phases), 'Through his telescope, Galileo saw four moons orbiting Jupiter, not Earth' (another mismatch with 'everything circles Earth').
Watch mismatches accumulate until a REVISE option becomes available; choose to revise, swapping in the Sun-centred model.
Re-test the revised Sun-centred model against each of these earlier observations and confirm that it now accounts for all three.
Note that the Sun-centred model is itself a new best-current explanation — stronger because it fits more evidence, but still open to further revision, not a final perfect answer.
At the end, sort statements into 'this is our best-supported explanation, open to revision' versus 'that's just an opinion', so provisional is never mistaken for 'anything goes'.
activities.insight: Revision is an evidence-driven mechanism: the old idea was the best explanation for the evidence people HAD, and when better evidence arrived science did not collapse — it upgraded and became stronger. The new model earns its place by accounting for the observations the old one could AND the ones it could not, while itself remaining a best-current explanation open to revision.

activities.title: Interview a scientist who lived a revision
steps: Take the role of an interviewer and question a historical or expert figure at the moment an accepted worldview is crumbling (e.g. an astronomer as the geocentric picture breaks down).
Challenge the figure: ask why they are changing a belief they once held, and what specific evidence turned them.
Press for evidence, not just anecdote — ask 'what did you observe?' and 'why didn't the old idea fit?'
Ask whether being shown to be mistaken means they failed, and listen to them explain why revising an idea in light of evidence is the point of science, not a defeat.
activities.insight: Changing your mind in the light of evidence is honest and is what science is for; this builds the affective sense that openness to revision is a strength, told from inside a real human change of view.

activities.title: Gallery of overturned ideas
steps: Move through examples of scientific revision: Earth-centred to Sun-centred models, fixed continents to plate tectonics, and spontaneous generation to the explanation that new organisms come from existing living organisms.
For each exhibit, reveal in order: the old explanation, then the new evidence that broke it, then the revised explanation.
Read for each a note on why the change strengthened science, and look for the common pattern across all three.
activities.insight: Revision is normal and recurring across all of science, not a one-off embarrassment in one field; the same old-idea -> breaking-evidence -> revised-idea pattern repeats.

activities.title: Astronomy close-up: how the old and new models explained retrograde motion differently
steps: Examine how Mars appears to loop backwards when viewed from Earth. Compare how an Earth-centred model uses epicycles to represent this observation with how a Sun-centred model explains it through the relative motions of Earth and Mars.
Compare how the Sun-centred arrangement, with Earth also moving, explains the apparent loop as a viewing effect of two moving bodies.

Explain how both models account for the apparent loop, and describe how Earth overtaking Mars provides the Sun-centred account. Consider this alongside the other observations in the activity rather than treating retrograde alone as decisive proof.
activities.insight: Different models can account for the same observation in different ways. Here the Sun-centred arrangement explains Mars’s apparent backward loop through relative motion, while Earth-centred models used epicycles; judging the models involves a wider body of evidence.

activities.title: Explain and sort: check the understanding
steps: Answer 'why did scientists change this idea?' for a revision you have met, naming the specific evidence that forced the change.
Match old ideas to the evidence that revised them.
Sort statements into 'best current explanation (evidence-based, open to revision)' versus 'just an opinion / anything goes'.

Respond in writing to the prompt: 'Long ago most people, including most scientists, were sure the Sun moved around the Earth; now we say the Earth moves around the Sun. Does that mean the old scientists were foolish? And might what scientists tell us today change too? Explain your thinking.'
activities.insight: Demonstrate that you can hold BOTH that the old view was reasonable for its evidence AND that current views remain open to revision, while keeping provisional distinct from mere opinion.

checkQuestion: Long ago, everyone — including scientists — was sure the Sun moved around the Earth. Now we say the Earth moves around the Sun. Does that mean the old scientists were bad at science, or foolish? And does it mean that what scientists tell us today might change too? Explain your thinking.
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning holds that the old scientists reasoned honestly from the evidence they had — the Sun does appear to cross the sky — and were not foolish: their idea was the best explanation for the evidence available. It sees revision as a strength of science, not a failure: ideas change because new evidence, or a better interpretation of the same evidence, arrives, and today's ideas are 'the best so far', still open to revision if evidence demands. It rejects both 'they were just stupid' and 'science is now finished and certain'.
